translations.text: Jesus took his twelve disciples: and the rest.
Here it is read in this gospel, which we have just heard from the deacon's mouth, that "the Saviour took his twelve disciples aside,
and said to them, Behold, we must go to the city of Jerusalem, and then all the things that were written about me by the prophets will be fulfilled.
"I shall be betrayed to the nations, and they will treat me with scorn, and scourge me, and afterwards kill me, and I will rise from death on the third day."
Then his disciples had no understanding of these words. Then it happened that they drew near to a city called Jericho, and a certain blind man was sitting there by the road;
and when he heard the people going along with the Saviour, he asked who was passing there.
They told him that it was the Saviour passing. Then he began to cry out, and said, "Saviour, Son of David, have mercy on me."
The people who were going ahead of the Saviour rebuked the blind man, telling him to be silent.
Then he cried out much more loudly, "Saviour, Son of David, have mercy on me." Then the Saviour stood still and ordered the blind man to be led to him.
When he drew near, the Saviour asked him, What do you want me to do for you?
He said, Lord, that I may see. And the Saviour said to him, Look now: your faith has healed you.
And he at once saw, and followed the Saviour, and glorified him. Then all the people who saw that miracle praised God with great fervour."
The beginning of this gospel touched on our Saviour's passion, yet he did not suffer at this time;
but he wished to make known his passion to his disciples far and long beforehand, so that they would not be too greatly frightened by the passion when the time came that he would suffer.

Their minds became frightened by Christ's saying, but he encouraged them again with the words he spoke, "I will rise from death on the third day." Then he wished to strengthen and confirm their faith with miracles.
And they then came to the place where the blind man sat by the road, and Christ healed him in the sight of the whole company, because he wished to bring them to faith by that miracle.
However, the miracles that Christ worked showed one thing through power, and signified another thing through mystery.

He truly worked those miracles through divine power, and with those miracles he confirmed the people's faith; but yet there was another thing hidden in those miracles, according to the spiritual sense.
This one blind man signified all mankind, which was blinded through Adam's sin, and thrust out of the joy of paradise, and brought into this life, which is compared to a prison.
Now we are locked out from the heavenly light, and in this life we cannot enjoy the eternal light; nor do we know any more of it than as much as we read in books through Christ's teaching.
This world, though it may sometimes seem pleasant, is nevertheless no more like the eternal world than a prison is like bright daylight.
All mankind was, as we said before, blinded with unbelief and error; but through Christ's coming we were drawn out of our errors and enlightened through faith.
Now we have the light in our minds, which is faith in Christ; and we have the hope of the joy of eternal life, though we still dwell bodily in our prison.
The blind man sat at the city called Jericho. Jericho is interpreted as, and means, 'moon.' The moon both waxes and wanes: for half the month it is waxing, for half it is waning.
Now the moon signifies our mortal life and the decay of our mortality. At one end people are born; at the other end they pass away.
When Christ came to the city of Jericho, which signifies the moon, then the blind man received sight.
The man who knows nothing of the eternal light is blind; but if he believes in the Saviour, then he sits by the way.
It often happens, when a man wants to turn away from evil, and atone for his sins, and turn to God with all his mind, that the old sins which he committed before come
and trouble his mind, and want to silence his voice, so that he does not call out to God. But what did the blind man do when the people wanted to silence him?

If, then, we persevere in our prayers, we can bring it about with our crying out that the Saviour, who was walking on before, stands still and will hear our calling, and enlighten our hearts with good and pure thoughts.
He said to the blind man, "What do you want me to do for you?" Do you think that he who was able to heal him did not know what the blind man wanted?
but let us ask our Lord for light: not the light that comes to an end, that is driven away by the night, that is common to us and to beasts;
Now I say to that man that the things he understands and can perceive, he does not perceive through his body but through his soul; and yet no one sees his soul in this life.
He who owns all things had only as much as he cared to have, and lived on other men's possessions.
Truly it is written, "Whoever wishes to be a friend of this world will be counted God's enemy."
Christ said in a certain place that "The way that leads to the kingdom of heaven is very narrow and steep; and the way that leads to the torment of hell is very wide and smooth."
We cannot do these things without hardships; but if we do them, then with those labours, through God's help, we can climb the steep way that leads us to eternal life.
So let us take the harder way, so that we toil here for a while, in order that we may be without toil for ever.
He who is unwilling to suffer anything in this life will have to suffer worse sufferings against his will in the life to come.
